- If sentiment is strongly negative (e.g., < -0.3) in recent days, model tends to overcorrect upward — reduce forecast slope or cap upward momentum.
- If sentiment is strongly positive (e.g., > 0.7) and price is falling, model often underreacts — increase downward bias or add early momentum correction.
- When true price drops sharply after a spike, model often overshoots downward — adjust forecast to be more volatile or add lagged support.
- If model forecast is rising steadily with low sentiment, it often fails to account for mean reversion — reduce forecast slope or add downward bias after 3–5 days of upward trend.
- If sentiment is neutral or mixed (±0.2–0.5), model tends to overestimate volatility — smooth forecast curve or reduce amplitude.
- If true price is below 50% of historical range, model often overestimates recovery — cap forecast at 10–15% above recent low.
- If sentiment turns negative after a spike, model often fails to recognize reversal — add early reversal signal or reduce forecast slope after sentiment drop.
- If model forecast is flat or rising slowly while sentiment is rising, it often misses downward breakout — add downward bias or reduce forecast slope after sentiment peak.
